clues: Ancient Egyptians recognized signs of this condition but had no medical solutions. They declared that 'only magic can cure' these although occasionally suggested to 'treat it with a knife and burn it with a fire so that it bleeds not too much'

Albert Einstein had this condition and underwent a surgical procedure where the affected area was wrapped in cellophane, intended to cause scarring and preventing expansion. This actually allowed him to survive for several more years.

Patients with connective tissue disorders are at higher risk of developing these. If they rupture, overall mortality is roughly 80-90% with about half of all patients dying before they reach the hospital

A famous early story of this disease was of Mr. McBean. His physician noticed that his urine grew remarkably thick and cloudy when heated, but cleared up completely when boiled further. While this boiling test was used to diagnose patients for generations, it is no longer used today as more sensitive tests were developed

In 1992, a man named James Bond from Ohio was diagnosed with this disease. At the time, the median survival was 2-3 years. Refusing to give up, he underwent 4 separate stem cell transplants and 6 clinical trials. In 2002, he entered a clinical trial for a drug with the code name 'trial 007'. He lived for more than 29 years post-diagnosis
Don't feel crabby if you haven't gotten it yet. 'Trial 007' was for bortezomib, which went on to revolutionize care of this disease globally.

A prominent Italian anatomist first documented these in 1564 but early scientists had no idea what they did. For nearly two centuries, they believed these were hollow capsules filled with black bile and called them capsulae atrabiliariae

In the 1800s, scientists realized that removing these was rapidly fatal. A French physiologist Brown-Séquard became obsessed with the idea that these structures secreted a mysterious, life-extending force. He famously experimented on himself by injecting liquid extracts from animals, claiming it was an anti-aging elixir that restored his youthful vigor
Despite weighing just a fraction of an ounce, these glands control vital functions like blood pressure, metabolism, and your 'fight-or-flight' response
In the 2nd century CE, the Greek physician Aretaeus of Cappadocia gave this disease its name meaning 'siphon' or 'to pass through', believing that 'the epithelial flesh and limbs melt into urine'

In ancient India, physicians noticed that the urine of patients with this disease attracted swarms of ants. They called the condition madhumeha, meaning 'honey urine'. Dr. Willis, an English physician also described the urine as 'wonderfully sweet, as if it were imbued with honey or sugar'

An estimated 830 million people worldwide have this condition and it is the leading cause of blindness in adults under the age of 65. It also can lead to lower extremity amputations, heart attacks, and kidney disease

This medication was the center of an explosive medical-journalism scandal in 2006. A lawyer representing patients passed thousands of leaked internal Eli Lilly emails and documents to The New York Times. These documents revealed that executives downplayed the massive weight-gain side effects because of worries that it would damage sales. This led to a multi-million campaign by Eli Lilly to suppress the documents online which ultimately failed to stop numerous liability lawsuits.
This medication is frequently used off label for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, as an appetite stimulant in patients with anorexia or cachexia, and for agitation and delirium.

Similar to Clozapine but without the risk of agranulocytosis, this medication was one of the early mainstream psychiatric medications to utilize freeze-dried orally disintegrating tablet technology, meaning the pill dissolves on the tongue in seconds without needing water.
